paper_title: Robust Explanatory Analysis for Structured Optimization Networks (REASON) in Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We seek a hierarchical resolution of residual error under a composite learning objective as a principled mechanism for identifying and exploiting additional information, particularly under distribution shift and perturbation. Inspired by the System 1/System 2 paradigm, we formulate this principle as a two-loop mechanism serving a common inference goal. A fast, System 1-like loop resolves the residual addressable by the available evidence; the remaining epistemic residual triggers a medium speed, System 2-like loop that actively acquires additional evidence and measures its informational value through residual reduction. Over nested solution spaces, the medium-loop optimum is provably no worse than the fast-loop optimum. Experiments show that the resulting two-loop model consistently improves upon the fast loop at approximately half the computation of the medium loop, including under unseen corruptions, and, when provided a cleaner observation, outperforms staged classifiers and learning-to-defer methods at equal computational cost.

sections.content: ROBUST EXPLANATORY ANALYSIS FOR STRUCTURED OPTIMIZATION NETWORKS (REASON) IN LEARNING Vahid Jebraeeli1, Hamid Krim1, Keisuke Fujii2 1ECE Department, North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC, USA 2Graduate School of Informatics, Nagoya University, Nagoya, Japan vjebrae@ncsu.edu ahk@ncsu.edu fujii@i.nagoya-u.ac.jp ABSTRACT We seek hierarchical resolution of residual error under composite learning objective as principled mechanism for identifying and exploiting additional information, particularly under distribution shift and perturbation. Inspired by the System 1/System 2 paradigm, we formulate this principle as two-loop mechanism serving common inference goal. fast, System 1-like loop resolves the residual addressable by the available evidence; the remaining epistemic residual triggers medium speed, System 2-like loop that actively acquires additional evidence and measures its informational value through residual reduction. Over nested solution spaces, the mediumloop optimum is provably no worse than the fast-loop optimum. Experiments show that the resulting two-loop model consistently improves upon the fast loop at approximately half the computation of the medium loop, including under unseen corruptions, and, when provided cleaner observation, outperforms staged classifiers and learning-to-defer methods at equal computational cost. Index Terms: Two-loop model, selective prediction, active perception, adaptive computation, epistemic uncertainty. 1. INTRODUCTION While machine learning has achieved remarkable success, much of this progress has come at the expense of increasing model and sample complexity while still falling short on generalization. Transformers have partially advanced beyond this paradigm by explicitly modeling cross-contextual coherence through attention[1], thereby enabling modest but important form of relational reasoning. Yet this reasoning remains largely associative and compositional, rather than reflecting deeper structural organization of memory, inference, and adaptive computation. The notion of reasoning has long been regarded as an inseparable component of intelligent learning, yet its principled and coherent integration into learning systems has remained elusive. major conceptual breakthrough emerged from the work of Kahneman and Tversky[2], and the subsequent fastslow, or System 1/System 2, view of cognition, which provided simple yet powerful framework for rationalizing how learning and decisionmaking may operate across distinct computational regimes: fast, intuitive, and largely automatic process, complemented by slower, deliberative, and reasoning-intensive process. Complementarily, the consciousness-prior perspective [3] suggests that such higher-level processing may operate on selectively filtered subset of the available representation, with attention providing natural mechanism for funneling task-relevant information toward more deliberate reasoning. In different but related way, we propose learning as hierarchy of loops that resolve residual uncertainty over progressively richer solution spaces. The Fast Loop (FL) resolves errors addressable by the current amortized inference map, while persistent residuals activate Medium Speed Loop (MSL) that explores alternative reasoning trajectories without altering the underlying representation. Failure of this expanded search to sufficiently reduce the residual is then interpreted as evidence of representational limitation, ideally triggering creative loop that operates over an architectural state space to adapt the hypothesis class itself, third level we defer to future work. Our proposed approach shares with selective classification, failure detection, learning-to-defer, and adaptive-inference methods, the recognition at high level that computational effort should be non-uniform across samples. Classical reject-option and selective-prediction methods determine whether an inference should be accepted or withheld [4, 5], while failure-detection and calibration methods seek reliable indicators of when prediction is likely to be erroneous or out of distribution [6, 7, 8]. Learning-to-defer methods extend this principle by routing uncertain decisions to downstream expert or model [9, 10, 11], whereas staged and early-exit architectures adapt computational cost by allowing easy examples to terminate early and difficult examples to invoke additional processing [12, 13, 14]. Our formulation views failure beyond the criterion for rejection, deferral, or additional computation, but as structured residual which determines the type of computation subsequently activated. Thus, rather than implementing confidence-based sequence of predictors of increasing complexity, the proposed hierarchy progressively expands the admissible modes of inference, reasoning, and representation according to the nature of the unresolved residual. To sum up and in contrast to fore-noted existing work hinging on pre-selected gating mechanism as well as to the Bayesian interpretation of System 1/System 2 in [15], the central objective of this paper is the realization of data-driven learning system inspired by the latter paradigm and built around two-loop learning architecture (Fast/Medium) resulting from hierarchical optimization formulation of learning functional objective. Our implementation also refers inputs by calibrated confidence threshold; what differs from prior gating is the action it triggers, the acquisition of new evidence. Two key questions are addressed in this contribution. First, can decision-making be improved by selectively acquiring additional evidence to reduce the residual error, rather than through uniformly optimized decision rule of comparable model complexity governed by preselected threshold gate? This directly examines the learning value of the System 1/System 2 paradigm, wherein additional computational and informational resources are invoked only when the fast-loop inference leaves significant unresolved residual, thereby allocating learning and reasoning resources where they are most needed. Second, what is the value of the MSL operating in REVEAL mode, where additional evidence is actively sought to resolve uncertainty remaining after fast-loop inference? The utility of the acquired evidence is measured by its informational novelty relative to the current representation and, critically, by its reduction of the epistemic residual Repi. It is thus assessed not by the mere acquisition of additional evidence, but by its ability to acquire informative evidence that measurably resolves epistemic uncertainty. Extensive experiments are conducted across four fine-grained recognition benchmarks: Stanford Dogs, CUB-200-2011, FGVC-Aircraft, and Oxford-IIIT Pets. Here, we shift focus from efficient learning with fixed data availability[16, 17] to inference, where computational and informational resources are rather adaptively allocated on per-input basis. The remainder of the paper formulates the problem and develops the proposed solution, presents the experimental results in Section 4, and concludes in Section 5. 2. PROBLEM STATEMENT AND SOLUTION 2.1. Residual decomposition over nested regimes We formulate learning as the hierarchical resolution of residual uncertainty over progressively richer solution spaces. FL, instantiated as conventional CNN, is trained to minimize the inference residual Rinf associated with the current inference map. Persistent residual uncertainty Repi activates MSL, which, upon request from the FL, explores alternative decisions using additional evidence. As noted earlier, the natural triggering of creative loop (CL) upon failure of these two procedures is deferred to future work. The FL processes each input and either adopts its decision (COMMIT) or, when confidence is insufficient, invokes the MSL to acquire and process additional evidence (REVEAL). The three cases provide objective benchmarks for evidence quality: the clean view establishes an upper bound, reprocessing the degraded input provides baseline, and an independent draw provides fresh evidence of the same quality. At set γ, all three options incur the same cost, so that any difference between them is attributable to the observation alone. 3. EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN Benchmarks. Four fine-grained benchmarks are used: Stanford Dogs [18], CUB-200-2011 [19], FGVC-Aircraft [20], and OxfordIIIT Pets [21] (Dogs, CUB, Aircraft, and Pets). Dogs is split per class into 14,355 training, 3,025 calibration, and 3,200 test images; its accuracies are therefore not comparable to published results. Its images are also drawn from ImageNet [22], which is part of the pretraining data of both backbones, so its absolute accuracies may be optimistic, although all compared models share this pretraining. The other three benchmarks retain their official test sets, with calibration sets of 1,200, 1,300, and 736 images held out from their training data, on which every operating point is selected and which no FL has seen. Models. The FL is MobileNetV3-Large [23] at 224 224 px (pixels), and the MSL is DINOv2-B [24] at 518 px, adapted with LoRA [25] and classifying by distance to class exemplars; both are fine-tuned once and then held fixed. The initial CUB and Aircraft FLs fell short of the published accuracy of their backbone and were therefore retrained with procedure selected on the calibration set, each test set being evaluated only once: clean accuracy rose from 68.31 to 81.72 on CUB and from 58.54 to 87.70 on Aircraft, against published values of 73.91 and 85.8 [26, 27]. The Dogs and Pets FLs are retained as initially trained: the Pets FL already exceeds its published value, and the Dogs FL is 5.1 points below linear classifier on its frozen backbone (1.5 for Pets). The single model of Section 4 is the same MSL retrained at 392 px under the identical protocol. Conditions. In addition to the clean images, seven perturbations of our own construction are applied, following [28]: occlusion at three sizes, cutout, feature-region masking, additive noise, and blur. Unless stated otherwise, each reported accuracy is the mean over these eight conditions, with the MSL reprocessing the degraded input. Equal cost. The three cases refer the same inputs in each condition and hence incur the same cost. The FL requires c1 = 0.22 GMAC per input (0.29 on CUB) and the MSL c2 = 154.94 GMAC. The operating point. The threshold c0 is chosen so that the MSL processes the half of the inputs for which the FL is least confident, i.e., γ = 1/2. This operating point is selected on the calibration set to maximize the gain over the FL while referring no more than half of the inputs to the MSL. Fig. 2. The FL alone, the two-loop model (FL + MSL), and the MSL alone, means over eight conditions (top), cost per input (bottom). Fig. 3. Staged classifiers [12] and learning to defer (best of three post-hoc rules [10, 11]), run with our FL and MSL at the same cost of about 78 GMAC per input, reprocess the input the FL saw, as in Fig. 2; ours receives clean view instead, so the gap measures the value of better evidence, acquisition cost excluded. Means over eight conditions. Training and testing. The FL and MSL are trained separately on each benchmarks training set, including images degraded by perturbations of the same types as the test conditions, and are then frozen. Using held-out calibration images never seen during training, c0 is set to the median FL confidence across all eight conditions. At test time, the FL first classifies every image: if its confidence is at least c0, the decision is retained (COMMIT); otherwise, the MSL processes second observation of the same object (the same degraded image, an independent draw of the same perturbation, or clean view), and its decision is used instead (REVEAL). Generalization beyond the eight conditions is evaluated by holding each condition out when setting c0 and by testing on fifteen corruption types unseen during training (Section 4.3). Performance differences are reported with 95 percent confidence intervals over test images. 4. RESULTS Sections 4.1 and 4.2 address the two questions of Section 1 in turn, and Section 4.3 tests generalization. 4.1. Accuracy and Cost Fig. 2 sets the FL, the two-loop model (FL + MSL) and the MSL side by side, with their respective cost; every model processes the degraded input. Analysis. The two-loop model improves on the FL on every benchmark, by 813 points when the MSL reprocesses the degraded input and by 1930 points when it processes clean view. With the degraded input, it comes close to the MSL alone on three benchmarks and exceeds it on Aircraft, at roughly half its cost  (Fig. 2)  . The confidence ranking accounts for less than half of this gain: against random referral of the same size, it adds 45 points with the degraded input and 57 with clean view. single model at the same cost. Retraining the MSL at 392 px, with all else unchanged, yields single model requiring 80.31 GMAC per input, slightly more than the two-loop model on three benchmarks. On the degraded input, it outperforms the two-loop model on Dogs, CUB, and Pets by 1.32.6 points and underperforms it on Aircraft by 3.6 points, all four differences being significant. Generalization Held-out conditions. Generalization is assessed by leaving one condition out at time [29, 30]: the threshold c0 is set to the median calibration confidence over the remaining seven conditions, and the two-loop model is tested on the held-out one. On every held-out condition, the two-loop model remains above the FL, on average by 813 points per benchmark when reprocessing the degraded input and by 1930 points with clean view. Unseen corruptions. Each benchmarks threshold c0 is then applied, unchanged, to the fifteen ImageNet-C corruption types [28] at severity three, generated with the implementation of [31]. The two-loop model outperforms the FL on every benchmark and corruption type  (Fig. 4)  ; it is within three points of the MSL alone on every benchmark and above it on Aircraft, at 5879 percent of its cost. The referral rate is not prescribed but follows from the threshold: on Dogs it ranges from 30 percent of the inputs under brightness to all of them under Gaussian noise, where the FL accuracy falls below one percent and the two-loop model then requires more computation than the MSL alone. Here too, an independent draw yields no gain. 5. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION Two-Loop Model: Strengths and Limitations. With fixed FLMSL pair, confidence-thresholded referral, and second observation acquired only when the FL is uncertain, the two-loop model gains 813 points over the FL at roughly half the MSL cost. The gain persists across all held-out conditions and an unseen corruption benchmark, exceeds random referral at matched cost, and satisfies the inequality of Section 2.1 on every benchmark. However, retraining the MSL at the computational cost of the two-loop model performs better on three of four benchmarks. The exception is precisely where the FL classifies its retained inputs more accurately than the MSL, condition detectable from calibration before training the alternative. Moreover, the benefit of the second observation arises primarily from improved quality rather than novelty. Since Eq. (7) assigns zero cost to evidence acquisition, selective acquisition is advantageous only when acquiring evidence itself carries cost, as when second viewpoint, higher-resolution or longer-exposure capture, or retake must be requested; otherwise, single model of the same computational cost is preferable. Running time and alternatives. In running time rather than arithmetic operations, the reduction is smaller: about 70 percent of the MSLs time on Dogs, rather than half. Given the same clean view, the FL alone still trails the two-loop model by 3.85.5 points. Future work. Two directions remain open: fusing both observations, and an epistemic-residual test that improves upon confidence. 6. COMPLIANCE WITH ETHICAL STANDARDS This study involved no human or animal subjects. It used four publicly available benchmarks of photographs of dogs, birds, aircraft, and pets [18, 19, 20, 21], the Stanford Dogs images being drawn from ImageNet [22], each used for non-commercial research under its license or terms of use, together with publicly released pretrained models [23, 24]. No data were collected and no live animals were involved. Some photographs incidentally show people; no individual was identified or analyzed, and no dataset images are reproduced in this paper. Ethical approval was therefore not required. 7.
